authors: Reuel, Anka and Hardy, Amelia and Smith, Chandler and Lamparth, Max and Hardy, Malcolm and Kochenderfer, Mykel J.
title: BetterBench: Assessing AI Benchmarks, Uncovering Issues, and Establishing Best Practices
venue_or_publisher: arXiv preprint (also NeurIPS 2024 Datasets and Benchmarks track, per proceedings listing in search results)
what_it_says: Scores 24 AI benchmarks against 46 criteria across design, implementation, documentation and maintenance. Finds wide quality variation, with 17 of 24 lacking easy replication scripts and 14 of 24 not reporting repeated runs or statistical significance.
why_relevant: Cite in Related work as evidence that the evaluations whose use the documents mandate or recommend are themselves of uneven quality, so a clause saying 'test' does not fix test quality. Differs: it assesses benchmarks, whereas this paper codes what documents require, and it does not code metric or threshold content.

authors: Bean, Andrew M. and Mahdi, Adam and others
title: Measuring what Matters: Construct Validity in Large Language Model Benchmarks
venue_or_publisher: NeurIPS 2025 Datasets and Benchmarks track (arXiv:2511.04703)
what_it_says: Systematic review of 445 LLM benchmarks from major venues. Finds that about 48 percent of the stated definitions of the target phenomenon are contested and only 16 percent use uncertainty estimates or statistical tests; proposes eight practices.
why_relevant: Use to support the Interpretation paragraph that binding text seldom says how to test: even where a test is run, construct validity is often weak. Also a close methodological neighbour, since it used a language model for screening followed by manual review and reports moderate reviewer agreement (mean Brennan-Prediger kappa 0.524), which can be set beside our coder agreement. Differs: it reviews research benchmarks, not regulatory clauses.

authors: Weidinger, Laura and Raji, Deb and Wallach, Hanna and Mitchell, Margaret and Wang, Angelina and Salaudeen, Olawale and Bommasani, Rishi and Kapoor, Sayash and Ganguli, Deep and Koyejo, Sanmi and Isaac, William
title: Toward an Evaluation Science for Generative AI Systems
venue_or_publisher: arXiv preprint
what_it_says: Perspective paper arguing that current generative AI evaluation is insufficient (static benchmarks with validity problems, audits that do not scale). Proposes borrowing from safety evaluation in transport, aerospace and pharmaceuticals, pairing pre deployment testing with post deployment monitoring.
why_relevant: Cite to frame why a table of where documents require testing matters: the science that would make a required test meaningful is still being built. Supports our coding of post deployment monitoring as a separate test type. Differs: it is a perspective piece with no document analysis.

authors: Rauh, Maribeth and Marchal, Nahema and Manzini, Arianna and Hendricks, Lisa Anne and Comanescu, Ramona and Akbulut, Canfer and Stepleton, Tom and Mateos-Garcia, Juan and Bergman, Stevie and Kay, Jackie and Griffin, Conor and Bariach, Ben and Gabriel, Iason and Rieser, Verena and Isaac, William and Weidinger, Laura
title: Gaps in the Safety Evaluation of Generative AI
venue_or_publisher: Proceedings of the AAAI/ACM Conference on AI, Ethics, and Society (AIES), vol. 7, pp. 1200-1217
what_it_says: Reviews more than 200 safety evaluations of generative AI and identifies three gaps: few evaluations for non text modalities, uneven coverage of ethical and social risks, and a focus on the model rather than its context of use.
why_relevant: Peer reviewed precedent for coding evaluations by category and reporting coverage gaps, and supports our observation that some test types (content safety, human oversight validation) are thin. Differs: it codes research evaluations, not clauses in regulation or guidance, and has no binding force dimension.

authors: Raji, Inioluwa Deborah and Xu, Peggy and Honigsberg, Colleen and Ho, Daniel E.
title: Outsider Oversight: Designing a Third Party Audit Ecosystem for AI Governance
venue_or_publisher: Proceedings of the 2022 AAAI/ACM Conference on AI, Ethics, and Society (AIES), p. 557
what_it_says: Compares third party audit systems in finance, environment and health regulation and argues that audits alone are unlikely to deliver accountability without deliberate institutional design.
why_relevant: Use in Related work for the third party audit ecosystem: our table records whether independent assurance is required or merely contingent (see the UAE paragraph). Differs: it argues from other regulated fields, while we count what AI documents currently say.

authors: Lewis, Dave and Lasek-Markey, Marta and Golpayegani, Delaram and Pandit, Harshvardhan J.
title: Mapping the Regulatory Learning Space for the EU AI Act
venue_or_publisher: arXiv preprint
what_it_says: Describes the AI Act as a framework for learning and sketches a space of system types, protections and learning activities. Notes that compliance leans on CEN/CENELEC JTC 21 and ISO/IEC standards, that participation of SMEs, civil society and academia is limited, and that most Annex III systems rely on self certification.
why_relevant: Supports the claim in Related work that the Act leaves much to the provider and that harmonised standards carry the detail on how to test; also supports our limit that standards behind paywalls were read only as catalogue pages. Differs: it is a legal and policy analysis, with no clause level table. Year and venue are not shown in the fetched text; confirm before citing.

authors: National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST)
title: Outline of Proposed Zero Draft for a Standard on AI Testing, Evaluation, Verification and Validation (TEVV)
venue_or_publisher: NIST AI Standards Zero Drafts project, outline for public comment
what_it_says: Outline of a high level TEVV standard loosely modelled on ISO/IEC 42001 and ISO/IEC/IEEE 29119-1, with clauses on terminology, concepts and governance and appendices of worked examples and a catalogue of methods. It is an outline for comment, intended to go to ISO/IEC JTC 1/SC 42.
why_relevant: Cite as a primary document that tells where the standards route for pre deployment testing is heading, and as a candidate row source for the table (check whether it is already a family member). Not scholarly and not peer reviewed; the date is inferred from the March 2025 project announcement and a September 2025 comment deadline.

authors: Gartlehner, Gerald and Kahwati, Leila and Nussbaumer-Streit, Barbara and Crotty, Karen and Hilscher, Rainer and Kugley, Shannon and Viswanathan, Meera and Thomas, Ian and Konet, Amanda and Booth, Graham and Chew, Robert
title: Commentary on data extraction with a large language model in evidence synthesis (as fetched at ebm.bmj.com/content/30/6/385; exact title and journal not shown in the fetched text)
venue_or_publisher: Probably BMJ Evidence-Based Medicine 30(6):385 (inferred from the URL only; not confirmed)
what_it_says: Commentary drawing on a proof of concept in which a model made 1 major and 5 minor errors against a human reference that itself held 21 minor errors; a repeat run weeks later gave similar error counts but in different data elements. Recommends adjudicating each human versus model discrepancy against the source report.
why_relevant: Directly supports our design: a verification audit against the source with an independent sample, and the point that the reference standard is itself fallible, which is why we call agreement among coders not accuracy. Differs: it concerns extraction from trial reports, not coding of clauses.

authors: Gartlehner, Gerald and others (full author list not shown in the fetched text)
title: AI-Assisted Data Extraction with a Large Language Model: A Study Within Reviews
venue_or_publisher: medRxiv preprint
what_it_says: Prospective study within six systematic reviews (63 studies, 9,341 data elements) comparing human only extraction with model extraction plus human verification. Error rates against an adjudicated reference were 9.0 percent for AI assisted and 11.0 percent for human only extraction, with fabricated data at 0.8 and 0.5 percent.
why_relevant: Gives measured error and fabrication rates to set beside our verification audit error rate, and supports keeping a human in the loop. Differs: measures a verify-then-correct workflow on trial data, whereas our verifiers are also language models and our remedy (human second coding of 100 rows) is still pending. Preprint; check for a journal version.

authors: Pangakis, Nicholas and Wolken, Samuel and Fasching, Neil
title: Automated Annotation with Generative AI Requires Validation
venue_or_publisher: arXiv preprint
what_it_says: Applies GPT-4 to 27 annotation tasks from 11 datasets and finds median accuracy 0.85 but median F1 0.71, with nine tasks below 0.5 on precision or recall. Sets out a workflow: codebook, human labelled random subset, comparison, codebook revision, held out check.
why_relevant: Strengthens the motivation for blind second codings and shows why we report percentage agreement beside kappa and F1 style checks. Our codebook then blind recode follows its steps; we differ in using language model second coders rather than expert human labels, which is our stated limit.

authors: Flemyng, Ella and Noel-Storr, Anna and others, on behalf of the joint AI Methods Group of Cochrane, Campbell Collaboration, JBI and Collaboration for Environmental Evidence
title: Position statement on artificial intelligence (AI) use in evidence synthesis across Cochrane, the Campbell Collaboration, JBI, and the Collaboration for Environmental Evidence 2025
venue_or_publisher: JBI Evidence Synthesis 23(11):2162-2166 (published jointly in several journals)
what_it_says: States that AI in evidence synthesis needs human oversight, that authors stay responsible, and that any AI making or suggesting judgments (eligibility, extraction) must be reported with tool, version, purpose and limitations. Requires evidence the tool is sound, with piloting or calibration where needed.
why_relevant: Authority for our disclosure in the Ethics section and for reporting the model assisted steps in detail. We can state which items of its reporting list our paper meets and which not (for example tool version and dates). Differs: it is a position statement, not an empirical study.

authors: Gallifant, Jack and Afshar, Majid and Ameen, Saleem and others, Bitterman, Danielle S.
title: The TRIPOD-LLM Statement: A Targeted Guideline For Reporting Large Language Models Use
venue_or_publisher: medRxiv preprint; peer reviewed version in Nature Medicine (per note on the fetched page; details not checked)
what_it_says: A reporting guideline for biomedical studies using language models: a checklist of 19 main items and 50 subitems built by an expedited Delphi process, stressing transparency, human oversight and task specific performance.
why_relevant: Use as the closest best practice for reporting language model assisted methods; we can map our disclosure to its items in an appendix. Differs: aimed at studies that evaluate or deploy models in biomedicine, not at using models as research assistants for document coding. Cite the Nature Medicine version after checking it.

authors: Gebru, Timnit and Morgenstern, Jamie and Vecchione, Briana and Vaughan, Jennifer Wortman and Wallach, Hanna and Daume III, Hal and Crawford, Kate
title: Datasheets for Datasets
venue_or_publisher: arXiv preprint v8 (journal version believed to be Communications of the ACM 2021; not confirmed from the fetched text)
what_it_says: Proposes that each dataset ship with a datasheet answering questions on motivation, composition, collection, preprocessing, uses, distribution and maintenance. The authors say the process should not be automated.
why_relevant: Frame for the documentation of the evidence table itself: our repository records licence terms, retrieval dates and a decision log, and a datasheet appendix would map to those. Differs: it concerns machine learning datasets; our table is a research dataset about documents.

authors: Nosek, Brian A. and Ebersole, Charles R. and DeHaven, Alexander C. and Mellor, David T.
title: The Preregistration Revolution
venue_or_publisher: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences (venue and year taken from the DOI shown in search results, not from the fetched copy)
what_it_says: Argues that fixing questions and analysis plans before seeing outcomes keeps prediction and postdiction apart. Lists practical problems, including pre existing data, where blinding is often partial.
why_relevant: Supports our explicit statements that baselines and the keyword lexicon were written by an analyst who had seen the table, so they are not preregistered, and that the verification sample was drawn independently. Differs: we did not preregister the main analysis; the paper should say so.

authors: van Miltenburg, Emiel and van der Lee, Chris and Krahmer, Emiel
title: Preregistering NLP Research
venue_or_publisher: Proceedings of NAACL 2021 (ACL Anthology 2021.naacl-main.51, per search results)
what_it_says: Offers preregistration templates for NLP work, including error analysis and resource papers with questions on sampling and annotator reliability, and notes that registration cannot prevent fraud or foresee every decision.
why_relevant: Peer reviewed precedent in the computational evaluation field for committing protocols before running them; we cite it when stating which parts of our protocol were committed with the code and which were not. Differs: it proposes templates and has no empirical test.

authors: Hofman, Jake M. and Chatzimparmpas, Angelos and Sharma, Amit and Watts, Duncan J. and Hullman, Jessica
title: Pre-registration for Predictive Modeling
venue_or_publisher: arXiv preprint (venue not stated in the fetched text)
what_it_says: Adapts preregistration to predictive modelling with a two phase template covering splits, metrics and baselines before training, and the model and test set statement before testing. In a study with six students it found people re-accessed test data after poor results.
why_relevant: Closest match to our baseline protocol (fixed folds, leave one family out, methods committed with code). We can cite it to explain the gap between a committed protocol and a true preregistration. Differs: it is for predictive modelling on fixed data, and we classify rows labelled by the same analyst.

authors: Li, Dan and Kanoulas, Evangelos
title: When to Stop Reviewing in Technology-Assisted Reviews: Sampling from an Adaptive Distribution to Estimate Residual Relevant Documents
venue_or_publisher: ACM Transactions on Information Systems 38(4), Article 41
what_it_says: Estimates the total number of relevant documents by sampling with replacement from an adaptive distribution with Horvitz-Thompson style estimators, and stops review at a target recall. Estimates tend to be low at low target recall.
why_relevant: Better developed alternative to capture recapture for our completeness check, which we describe as a simpler pilot against an independent reference list; it also shows why our estimate is likely to be an upper bound on completeness. Differs: it assumes a ranker over a known candidate pool, which we do not have for a sampling frame of policy documents.

authors: Alzubaidi, Ahmed and Alsuwaidi, Shaikha and Boussaha, Basma El Amel and AlQadi, Leen and Alkaabi, Omar and Alyafeai, Mohammed and Alobeidli, Hamza and Hacid, Hakim
title: Evaluating Arabic Large Language Models: A Survey of Benchmarks, Methods, and Gaps
venue_or_publisher: arXiv preprint (Technology Innovation Institute, Abu Dhabi)
what_it_says: Reviews about 41 Arabic LLM benchmarks in four categories, among them safety and hallucination. Finds uneven dialect coverage, cultural misalignment in translated sets, no standard hallucination benchmark and roughly a quarter of benchmarks private or partial.
why_relevant: Supports our finding that no row requires language specific performance testing: the research side also shows thin Arabic evaluation. Differs: it surveys benchmarks, not regulatory requirements, and says nothing on binding force. Authors are at a UAE institute; note when citing.

authors: Peppin, Aidan and Kreutzer, Julia and Schoenauer Sebag, Alice and Marchisio, Kelly and others, Hooker, Sara
title: The Multilingual Divide and Its Impact on Global AI Safety
venue_or_publisher: arXiv preprint (Cohere Labs); venue not stated
what_it_says: Argues that safety work and evaluation data concentrate on English and a few high resource languages, so safeguards are weaker elsewhere, and that translated safety prompts can lose their harmful intent. Recommends locally grounded evaluation data and transparency about language coverage.
why_relevant: Provides the rationale for coding language specific testing as its own question in the UAE section; Arabic appears only in passing as one of eight languages of a red teaming set. Differs: a policy primer, not a document analysis.

authors: Belabes, Abderrazak
title: An analytical framework for an ethics of AI in Saudi Arabia beyond principles underpinning privacy and the protection of personal data
venue_or_publisher: Journal of the College of Law (Majallat Kulliyyat al-Huquq), King Abdulaziz University
what_it_says: Proposes an AI ethics framework for Saudi Arabia that goes beyond privacy to religious, moral and societal values, reviews the national institutional and regulatory setup, and compares Saudi AI ethics principles with UNESCO recommendations.
why_relevant: Adds Saudi Arabia scholarship to the Gulf paragraph beside the GCC and UAE works already cited; shows attention to principles rather than testing requirements, supporting our statement that we found no study of Gulf testing requirements. Differs: ethics and principles, not testing. Read from the abstract page only; the journal interface is in Arabic.
